intro:
John the apostle writes 1 John around AD 85-95 from Ephesus to churches facing the first full-blown heresy: Gnosticism. False teachers (secessionists) have left the community, denying Jesus came in flesh (Docetism) and claiming special knowledge ('gnosis') that lets them sin without consequence. They also lack love for fellow believers.

John writes to reassure genuine believers ('I write so you may know you have eternal life') and expose counterfeit Christianity. Three tests emerge: doctrinal (confessing Jesus came in flesh), moral (obeying God's commands), and social (loving fellow Christians). The famous 'God is love' statements come in context of distinguishing true from false community.

The letter is cyclical, repeating themes with deepening intensity rather than linear argument. John contrasts light/darkness, truth/lie, love/hate, children of God/children of devil. He addresses three life stages ('children,' 'young men,' 'fathers') with appropriate encouragement. The tone is pastoral yet firm—John writes as the last living apostle defending apostolic witness.
outro:
John concludes with stark contrasts: 'We know that anyone born of God does not continue to sin... the whole world is under control of evil one.' Final assurance: 'We know that the Son of God has come and given us understanding so we may know him who is true.'

1 John became the church's manual for discernment in times of theological confusion. Its simple yet profound tests—truth, obedience, love—cut through complex heresies. The emphasis on tangible love ('let us not love with words but actions') keeps Christian ethics grounded in incarnation.

Written when Christianity was separating from both Judaism and early heresies, 1 John defines essential Christianity: Christological confession producing ethical transformation within loving community. Its assurance of salvation ('you may know') has comforted believers doubting their standing before God.
